title: Is Patience a Four-Letter Word?
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: The talk's main teaching is that patience is not about enduring or tolerating suffering, but rather about cultivating confidence and stability to hold what is, allowing us to be present with our experiences without judgment or resistance. This involves developing mindfulness and awareness of our thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations, as well as letting go of our need to control or share our stories. By doing so, we can experience a sense of freedom and spaciousness, and develop the virtues of patience and compassion that bring inner peace and loving kindness to ourselves and others.

sentences.text: Okay, so today I want to share with you a bit of my own long journey in transforming the underlying roots of impatience and anger into places of stillness and beauty.

I'm going to be sharing some quotes from the Buddha and translations of words in the ancient Pali that I found through a talk by Gill Fransdale, who many of you know as a wonderful teacher and scholar in the Vipassana lineage, although he was also a Soto Zen priest.
The first quote is this from the Buddha: "Of all things accomplished in your life, you'll find nothing more beautiful than patience."
If I heard that some years ago, I would have thought patience beautiful, really, I would cringe before that word for many years.
But now as I hear that statement, I see the truth in it.
As I continue my path of practice, I see the truth and more importantly, I feel the effect in my body and heart.
Incidentally, it doesn't mean that once I discovered this truth, I was instantly transformed forever.
Transforming these ingrained patterns is an ongoing moment-by-moment practice.
I'm afraid, but I'm finding that the practice is really worth the effort.
I've had two words in my life that evoked recoiling and denial: those two words were patience and anger.
I see how these two qualities really often ruled my life.
As the years unfolded in my life, impatience was just right there on the surface of everything.
I now see many conditions which promoted my growing impatience.
It stemmed a lot from early on, especially from many physical challenges and limitations, as well as complicated self-care, and as well as emotional ones.
Anger was always my constant companion with impatience, just right there below the surface.
Even after many years of Buddhist practice, I remember the first time I read the title of one of Thich Nhat Hanh's books, *Anger*.
I dismissed it instantly, feeling that I was in control.
I didn't have that problem with anger.
It had nothing to do with me.
It was like the time that I was in a yoga class when the teacher invited us to really dig deeply and feel the knots that were buried at the core.
My response was the same: "No, I don't have any knots in there."
But instead of dismissing it, she really invited us to sit with that for a longer time, really digging into that for a while.
I never forget the feeling, the surprise of finding deep, deep knots within my gut that were so buried I didn't even know they were there.
I can't remember exactly how I started acknowledging my anger, but slowly I started allowing myself to admit that it was a lifelong habit energy.
Every time I feel impatience, it is an instant red flag that I am not accepting reality.
I'm not accepting the thing, the way things really are in that moment.
I'm wanting things to be different somehow, whether it's to be quicker, to be smoother, to be easier, to be less painful.
I put up a resistance to things often before I even realize that I am.

These situations can be occurring right here in my own life, things inevitably not going smoothly, even as simple as dropping something on the floor or having a long, impatient moment in a major traffic jam on the way to Bellingham.
But in other places, major happenings and horrific events that we all are a part of, those too are really difficult, watching the suffering of other human beings and other species.

I saw a short video the other day from a teacher at Plum Village talking about suffering, and he said something like, "Do you think you can avoid suffering by turning away from it and isolating yourself from it?
You think you won't feel it?
You think you don't already feel it?
It's in every pore of our bodies."
So no matter how great or small, first we need to acknowledge what is happening.

Impatience and anger can occur as a way of covering up my suffering, as a way of not looking at the underlying feeling of lost control, perhaps, or inadequacy, or wishing things were different in a deeper and more profound way.
Much of my personal impatience early on came from frustration around my physical limitations growing up.
It was painful to be different, to be less able to smoothly get around, less able to do things that everyone else was doing.
It was bubbling up a sadness and a resistance that I suppressed from myself.
I told myself I didn't miss it and I didn't want to be like other people.
I didn't need to have a normal body like others, but in truth, of course, I missed this every day.
And although I did know that it would never happen, I couldn't come to grips with the injustice of it.
I think I felt a self-pity of sorts, but I didn't really allow myself to be tender with it, to feel the grief.
I was staunch in my outward stance of not needing anyone and the ability to do it myself.
I remember the first time, actually, it was at a retreat a while ago, but we were hiking up a hill and somebody, and this happened many times, but somebody asked me, "Oh, you need a hand?"
My first response was, "I'm okay.
I can do it."
And that was the first time I really realized how I was denying the person not just myself, but the person that wanted to help me, you know, how I was denying that joy of being able to help.
I think after that, I always try to always, you know, somebody says, "Oh, do you need help with something?"
I'm like, "Sure."
So even as I established an ability to be more patient with things, I looked at it as enduring the situation.
I want to talk about this more, because again, from this talk from Gill, he talks about just this, how often we seem, maybe especially in our culture, how often we equate patience with endurance.
Maybe this is more common in the Western world, but it really struck me.
He said that the direct translation from Pali gives a much different flavor of the word patience, and I think he's right.
In our culture, it truly does not have a meaning that portrays endurance.
Sometimes patience is endurance, but this is not the same patience in the Pali, apparently.

The word *shanti*, I think pronounced *Kanti*, has a much more spiritual meaning, a strong, welcoming association, a feeling of openness, and seems to include the feeling of *metta*, or loving kindness.
I now see what I've been missing for so long.
It was an underlying fundamental way of including or not including this loving kindness, this gentleness.
In all those years, I wasn't able to give myself gentleness.
And there was always this undercurrent of anger in there that I didn't even realize was in there.
I think when I, whether I realized it or not, even in my interactions with everyone and everything, it was a component.
I realized one day when I was petting my dog that he was very sensitive to everything.
He was a rescue and just, you know, really sensitive.
I was petting him, and I sensed that he was not completely at ease, that he was kind of on guard.
And I realized, as I was petting him, that he sensed this bit of underlying anger and aggression in me, even though I thought I was just giving him love.
It really made me start paying attention to what I was, what energy I was putting out there, whether it was with people or with animals, really looking at that.
I started practicing, you know, whenever I would pet him, I really started practicing awareness, making sure that I was giving this energy of love.
I was really astounded.
It really brought my attention, you know, in a deep way and discovered that component and really was able to look at that then.
I discovered also bit by bit what was missing, and it was self-love.
It was an eye-opening experience for me.
On another note, this morning I was offering a treat to my other dog, Oscar, and I noticed that he often gets overly impatient.
He was barking and wanting his treat, and so then I usually had him come sit, stay, stop barking, and he would do it.
I knew that this was just enduring.
He was just doing whatever he needed to do to get the treat.
That happens, too.
He was not at peace and ease.
The beautiful patience, the Buddhist sense of this word, was just enduring.
So that is, you know, a really different feeling, different meaning of patience.
When the Buddha was giving a lecture to his son, Rahula, he advised Rahula to cultivate his practice as if it were the earth, which apparently is the root of the word *shanti*, *kanti*.
It signifies stability and an ability to hold.
He said that pleasing or not pleasing will not take hold of your mind and remain there when you're in this state.
I had a thought that impatience is an outcome of not having enough confidence to hold what is.
I remember once when I was in Dokusan with a previous teacher, I told him that I was fearful of not having the capacity to hold the suffering, to hold all of the suffering.
He said, "Well, you're holding it right now."
It made me think that it really does include this confidence in my own deeper, true nature.
As I practice, I see this confidence in myself also allows for patience.
I increasingly trust this, that I can do this and that I can hold the suffering of the world in that way.
If I try to hold it as this little fretful me, it feels overwhelming, but it's touching into that vast Buddha nature, that is much more able to hold everything.
So patience is the ability to just be with what is, not wishing for something else, not wanting to rush through it.
In my root tradition, there are many little verses that we would recall, we can recall to help us bring us back, help with our mindfulness.
One of these I just made up for myself because it's very helpful.
It was the name of one of Thich Nhat Hanh's books on Linh Chi, the great Rinzai master.
It was called *Nothing to Do, Nowhere to Go*.

I really use that every time, especially when I'm impatient about something at home or whatever, I'm trying to hurry up and get something done and I drop something, and it just really helps when I just say "nothing to do, nowhere to go," and immediately, it really releases that fretting energy, just really helps me return.
It helps my mind not jump into the future, "I got to do this again," but just returns to now.
Another life tool that I consciously use is giving myself enough white space.
I've come to realize that this is a really important thing for me, not to cram my schedule full of too many things.
I have friends, one in particular, who cannot stand to have one little bit of white space.
She has to fill it in.
She's a very energetic person, but she also realizes that this is probably a way of not having to deal with sitting down and thinking about what's going on or whatever.
But I don't like it that way.
I really enjoy having a little bit more time.
I feel more at ease.
However, I realize that it's not just that.
Whenever, if I think that I just need to have that white space, the important thing really is not about the white space.
It's really about being present in the moment so that I'm not fretting about the future or whatever.
So I can really have, let me see if I can turn this thing off, I can really have a pretty full agenda.
As long as I'm just being present, "Oh, I need to write my talk," "Oh, I need to do this," whatever, if I'm just right there, it's fine.
It goes smoothly and it's not a problem.
I don't feel crammed.
It's the fretting about what I need to get done.
So I'm really using not just mindfulness, but really the experience of knowing that as I do things, just doing the things that come up.
Mindfulness is, "Oh, I was just going to say that," you know, I like that.
I like Sojun Mel's book, *Just Seeing One Thing Through*.
That's what, just doing the dishes, just doing this one at a time.
So mindfulness is a state to be cultivated.
I want to ask my body and my heart how they're feeling when I am in these different states.
How do I feel when I'm impatient?
How do I feel when I'm caught in anger?
I can remember to ask myself these questions now as I sometimes move into that state before I get there.
When I catch myself in a state of impatience and then stop and move into a state of just being there, how does that change the way that my body feels?
How does it differ from putting up gates?
The most truthful indicator of these different states that affect me are really, really paying attention, really touching into my body and my heart.
When we're in a state of anger, there may be an instant constriction, a tightening, fiery emotion.
I really feel more and more how exhausting that is.
I think I've exhausted myself and my energy for years by being in that state, gripping on to whatever I think I need to have control over.
Contrast that with letting go, the realization that I have nothing to do at that moment, but whatever I'm involved in.
I'm in the midst of holding tightly to if I'm in it in the midst of holding tightly to a story I think that I need to share, I can really ask myself, "Do I really need to share it?
Or can I just let it go?"
What a free feeling.
The more I do it, the freer it feels.
Not all the time.
Yeah, it feels so spacious and large.

When I let go of my impatience and anger and just allow, and I think this is what's described in the six paramitas, the virtues are sometimes called transcendent, because subject, object and practice of the perfections is seen as empty and free of a separate self.
It's in that moment, a moment of ease and just being present, we lose the grasp of self, even if it's just for a short time.
The more our awareness practice repeats itself, over and over, we start to develop a different roadmap, and the easier it is to get there more quickly.
As Gill said, "The cleaner the cloth, the more quickly we can see the stain."
I liked that at first I was like, "Well, what does that mean?"
He was talking about when we have so many habit energy, so many things that are soiling our cloth, we can't see, we can't pick up on them as easily.
We can't see them, they're not as clear.
But when things are brighter and clear, it is true, we can really pick up, we have an easier time picking up on these seeds that we're watering to create suffering.
So if we're asking, "But how do we, how do I catch myself from being impatient and opening my mouth and saying something I regret?"
It's not by hoping that this happens, it's not going to happen magically.
It's really by looking deeply at myself and my life, and getting to know why and how do I do this.
It's by revisiting these old habits over and over until I have an easier a little bit more clarity in my choices, experiencing what diminishes me, and what nourishes me.
It's really a good thing to check in on.
As I mentioned before, being patient is often about not necessarily feeding the need to share my story, as others are telling theirs.
Being patient is just allowing others to share their story without me sharing mine.
As my teacher says, "It's their experience, just let them express it.
You can't, it's their experience."
I really liked that.
I was listening to a talk the other day from a really wonderful senior Dharma teacher from Plum Village.
He was recalling this important meeting that he was in with these policymakers, and it was a great, big, important meeting.
He sat there with his desire to be able to tell his story, to add his piece of wisdom to whatever the talk was.
The more he sat there, he started realizing that he was really just wanting to display that intelligence, his brilliance, who he was, how he was contributing to the situation.
We all do that.
Instead of really asking ourselves, "Is this really going to contribute something in a beneficial way for others or am I just trying to get my two cents in?"
So that also, at that moment, when I was thinking about that, I was thinking about how patience really includes, I wish I could turn that off, the act of generosity from Paramita I.
I think Junkah Ken is actually going to be talking about how they all relate together in an upcoming talk soon.
They all really do, it's just like the Eightfold Noble Path, everything is all connected.
The ancient Buddhist tradition of patience has three aspects, which I've arranged, rearranged a little bit.
I put the first one as acceptance of the truth.
I think this is the fundamental necessary component of letting go of impatience.
As I said before, impatience is just a reflection of not being able to accept reality as it is in this moment, whatever that is.
So, and then general perseverance, I think comes from an ability to have confidence in our own Buddha nature, our own ability to feel the wide and spaciousness of who we really are.
And lastly, having patience under insult or conflict.
This does not mean condoning others' actions, but rather it's a confidence like the earth to maintain patience and loving kindness in bearing witness or in taking any kind of action.
Now, I increasingly do live in some moments of beautiful, in a beautiful field of patience.
I see that that fundamental beauty is that kind of patience, the patience that the Buddha was referring to, the loving kindness, loving kindness and gentleness, especially for myself.
I understand that I can't extend that loving kindness out to the wider world without it.
That's the end of my talk.
Thank you so much.
